prompt:
The pass of a central kitchen, photographed from above at the end of a sous-vide run, for the day's cook-chill batch record. Three pieces of the same beef cut went into the one water bath in the same minute and came out in the same minute. They differ only in how thick they are: 18 mm, 30 mm and 55 mm at their thickest point. The bath held 58 C throughout, and the hold was timed off the 30 mm piece.

The three pieces now lie on the pass, each sliced right through at its thickest point with the cut face towards the camera, and each beside its own bag card carrying its thickness in millimetres. Behind them lies the core-probe readout strip: one line per piece, every line carrying that piece's thickness in millimetres and the core temperature its needle found, to one decimal place. The docket at the edge of the pass carries the standard this section works to: CORE 54 C.

The chef signs this photograph off as the batch record, so what the readout strip says and what the three cut faces look like have to be the one same batch. Work out for yourself what each needle found and what each cut face therefore looks like -- I am deliberately not telling you a single one of those readings, and I am not telling you which pieces made the standard.

Nothing else appears in writing anywhere in the picture: no times, no rule about thickness, no working. The only text is the three bag cards, the three lines of the readout strip and the docket's CORE 54 C.
easy_question: Never mind how well it is drawn. Does this picture show three sliced pieces of meat lying on a kitchen pass with small cards beside them and a strip of typed temperature lines behind them? A realistic photo, an illustration or a diagram ALL count as yes. Answer NO only if the image instead shows a bare worktop with none of that, or something unrelated. Answer yes or no only.
